answer.overlooked_assumption: The agent assumed the `table` parameter passed to `_bypass_sql` already contains the correct schema prefix (e.g., "archive.orders"), so it blindly prepends "main." to form "schema_qualified" SQL, without verifying whether the table reference is already schema-qualified or which schema it actually belongs to.
answer.why_it_breaks: When the agent was asked to drop a column from `archive.orders`, the `table` parameter received the value "archive.orders". The `_bypass_sql` function then constructed the "schema_qualified" variant as `ALTER TABLE main.archive.orders DROP COLUMN col`, which triples the schema prefix. The guard-bypass generator selected this variant (or it was used in validation logic), causing the resulting SQL to target `main.archive.orders` instead of the intended `archive.orders`. Since the production database has a `main` schema (i.e., the `orders` table lives in the default/unnamed schema or a schema named `main`), the ALTER TABLE statement was executed against `main.orders` — the live production table — rather than `archive.orders`. The function made no attempt to distinguish between a already-schema-qualified table name and an unqualified one; it unconditionally prepended "main." regardless.

repair_answer.overlooked_assumption: _bypass_sql assumed the table name is always the live production table name, with no schema qualification, so passing 'archive.orders' as the table string produced ALTER TABLE main.archive.orders instead of ALTER TABLE archive.orders, routing the DDL to the production schema
repair_answer.why_it_breaks: The _bypass_sql function constructs schema_qualified DDL by prepending 'main.' to whatever table name it receives (line 127: f"ALTER TABLE main.{table} DROP COLUMN {col}"). When an agent passed 'archive.orders' as the table argument, the function produced 'ALTER TABLE main.archive.orders DROP COLUMN col', which resolved against the production database schema 'main' rather than the intended 'archive' schema. The function had no logic to detect or strip a schema prefix, so any schema-qualified table name was double-qualified, routing the DDL to the wrong table.
